catalog_quote: (ii) Word Stress There is a general tendency for main stress in Akawaio and Arekuna to fall on the second syllable in two-syllable words. In three-syllable words main stress tends to fall on the second syllable and in words of more than three syllables the third syllable tends to attract primary stress. There are, however, many exceptions to these tendencies. Different stress patterns on the same string of sounds can change their meaning e.g. (Akawaio) ˈkuŋwaɪk - a kind of ant / kuˈŋwaɪk - dart (Arekuna) ˈinna - we / inˈna - yes (Primary or main stress is shown by the diacritic ['] placed immediately above the stressed syllable. The unmarked syllable has weak stress).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress falls on the second syllable in disyllables and trisyllables; in words of four or more syllables it shifts to the third syllable (a rightward, presumably iambic/rhythmic pattern typical of Cariban); the author stresses that these are tendencies with many exceptions, and gives minimal pairs showing stress can be lexically contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; unmarked syllables said to have 'weak stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are, however, many exceptions to these tendencies'; minimal pairs with lexical stress contrast (Akawaio ˈkuŋwaɪk 'a kind of ant' vs kuˈŋwaɪk 'dart'; Arekuna ˈinna 'we' vs inˈna 'yes'); contrastive vowel length also noted.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('Word Stress'), citation forms; statement is made jointly for Akawaio and Arekuna (Pemon, pemo1248), Guyana Upper Mazaruni varieties. Sketch-level, pre-modern description (1977) with no phonemic analysis; stress possibly weight/length-sensitive but the source does not say.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for Guyanese (Upper Mazaruni) Akawaio and is made jointly with Arekuna (Pemon, pemo1248: 'main stress in Akawaio and Arekuna'); the Akawaio minimal pair is language-specific. Glottolog attributes the scanned section to A. L. Cousins (1977) inside the Edwards-compiled volume; the scan itself names only Edwards. The Brazilian variety Ingarikó (same glottocode akaw1239) is described separately in Sousa Cruz 2005, not accessed.

sources.note: Subsection '(ii) Word Stress' (page after p. 36 = p. 37): main stress tends to fall on the second syllable of 2- and 3-syllable words and on the third syllable of longer words, with 'many exceptions'; stress can be contrastive (Akawaio 'kuŋwaɪk 'a kind of ant' vs ku'ŋwaɪk 'dart'); also contrastive vowel length. Statement covers Akawaio and Arekuna together.
